report.summary: No system provides fully provably behaviour-preserving transformations for all Python features. Formal semantics exist (e.g. Politz et al. 2014, Guth et al. 2015) but have not been leveraged for a comprehensive refactoring tool. Conservative static analysis can catch some issues (e.g. variable capture in closures, mutable default aliasing, evaluation order changes), but guarantees are limited. Common refactorings like extract method, rename, and move are unsafe under closures, decorators, generators, name shadowing and side effects without careful checks. I recommend starting with a small set
risks: Formal semantics may not cover all Python constructs (e.g., certain decorators, metaclasses, C extensions).
Even proven transformations may have subtle interactions with dynamic features like introspection or monkey-patching.
User must accept a restricted subset of Python or annotate impure regions to retain safety.
todos: Implement a tiny set of safe transformations (e.g., local variable rename) using a formal model of Python's scoping and evaluation order; prove them correct.
Build a 'refactoring firewall' that rejects transformations unless the affected code passes a conservative side-effect purity analysis.
Integrate with a regression test runner to catch any unintended changes during development.

handoff.suggestion: Investigate the K-framework Python semantics (Guth et al., 2015) as a basis for modelling and proving transformations. Start with a minimal core calculus and extend only with features you can formally verify.

name: q36-semantics-preserving-transforms
question: Provably behaviour-preserving source transformations for Python specifically: which are actually safe given closures, mutable default arguments, decorators, generators, name shadowing and evaluation-order side effects? Which transformations look safe and are not?
